claude.sample_unit: simulated women per run (100 simulation runs)

links.outcome: Effect of error-rate parity mitigation on group mortality disparity and privileged group mortality
links.effect: EqOdds/EqOppTPR reduced mortality rate ratio from 3.77 to ~3.05-3.07 but raised privileged group mortality via leveling down; EqOppFPR slightly raised disparity (3.82).
links.quote: Although the reduced disparity in mortality rates implies a positive health equity outcome, it is notable that in the EqOppTPR and EqOdds scenarios, the privileged group's mortality rate increased (Fig. 2A ).

links.outcome: Simulated group-wise mortality and socioeconomic outcomes under fairness-constrained AI
links.effect: Stark mortality disparities persisted regardless of algorithmic fairness constraints; equalized odds reduced disparity by only ~12 per 100k versus ~57 per 100k from improving screening access.
links.quote: We observed stark differences in annual mortality rates between the privileged and unprivileged groups, regardless of the algorithmic fairness constraints imposed.

links.outcome: Fair distribution of AI-enabled care benefits when access barriers differ between groups
links.effect: Access barriers had greater impact on disparities than AI fairness; enforcing equalized odds reduced disparity ~12 per 100k vs ~57 per 100k with 93% screening access.
links.quote: The sensitivity analysis for parameters determining the likelihood of screening, treatment delays, and adjuvant treatment within the simulation showed that barriers to accessing appropriate healthcare had a greater impact on health disparities than AI-based interventions.

links.outcome: Effect of radiologist reliance on biased AI on mortality rate disparity
links.effect: Mortality rate disparity surged with higher reliance on AI under Naive and EqOppFPR scenarios (with TPR disparities); unaffected under EqOdds.
links.quote: Here, it can be seen that the mortality rate disparity surged with a higher degree of reliance on the AI system under both the Naive and EqOppFPR scenarios.

links.outcome: Impact of subgroup TPR/FPR disparities in AI on group-wise outcomes
links.effect: Lowering unprivileged TPR by 30% increased mortality rate ratio by over 15%; 30% higher privileged FPR reduced ratio by under 5%.
links.quote: For instance, at a given ΔFPR, lowering the TPR for the unprivileged group by 30% increased the mortality rate ratio by over 15%.

unlisted_practices: Using sociotechnical simulation to evaluate fairness metrics' effect on long-term outcomes
Prioritizing TPR parity over FPR parity in fairness targets
Addressing structural access barriers (screening access) alongside algorithmic fairness
Avoiding leveling-down fairness methods (e.g., Pareto fairness)

links.effect: EqOppFPR worsened ratio 3.82 vs 3.77 Naive; EqOppTPR/EqOdds reduced ratios to 3.05/3.07, with EqOdds reducing disparity 12.22 per 100k.
links.quote: This was reduced to 3.05 (95% CI:3.04, 3.06) and 3.07 (95% CI:3.06, 3.08) under the EqOppTPR and EqOdds algorithmic fairness scenarios, respectively.

links.effect: 30% lower unprivileged TPR increased mortality ratio over 15%; 30% higher privileged FPR caused less than 5% reduction.
links.quote: For instance, at a given ΔFPR, lowering the TPR for the unprivileged group by 30% increased the mortality rate ratio by over 15%.

links.effect: Average mortality-rate ratios were 3.77 Naive, 3.82 EqOppFPR, 3.05 EqOppTPR, and 3.07 EqOdds.
links.quote: We observed stark differences in annual mortality rates between the privileged and unprivileged groups, regardless of the algorithmic fairness constraints imposed.

links.effect: Increasing unprivileged screening from about 65% to 93% reduced Naive mortality disparity from 105.48 to 56.88 per 100k.
links.quote: In particular, when approximately 93% of the unprivileged group was able to be screened, the mortality rate disparity in the Naive scenario was reduced to 56.88 (95% CI:56.68, 57.08) per 100k, from 105.48 (95% CI:105.26, 105.71) per 100k in the baseline setting when approximately 65% of the unprivileged group was screened (illustrated in Fig. 2A ).

links.effect: Naive FNR privileged/unprivileged: 27.11/26.74 at α=0.0; 22.94/30.01 at α=0.5; 18.79/33.33 at α=1.0.
links.quote: Here, it can be seen that the mortality rate disparity surged with a higher degree of reliance on the AI system under both the Naive and EqOppFPR scenarios.

unlisted_practices: Increasing screening access for the unprivileged group
Reducing treatment delays for the unprivileged group
Increasing access to adjuvant treatment for the unprivileged group

models_evaluated: Simulated AI breast cancer screening model

links.outcome: breast cancer mortality rate disparity between groups
links.effect: Absolute reduction in mortality rate disparity was 12.22 (95% CI: 11.91, 12.53) per 100k for EqOdds vs naive, while mortality rate ratio was 3.82 for EqOppFPR vs 3.77 for naive.
links.quote: Comparing the Naive and EqOdds scenarios, this amounted to an absolute reduction in mortality rate disparity of 12.22 (95% CI:11.91,12.53) per 100k individuals.
